Listen to this article Share US Treasury net interest outlays exceed $1 trillion in fiscal 2026 US Treasury net interest outlays exceeded $1 trillion in fiscal 2026, making debt service one of the federal budget’s largest categories. The final Monthly Treasury Statement, issued in October 2026, also reports the year’s spending and deficit. Government borrowing also features in the monetary history examined by The Prehn Institute. Changes in monetary conditions can influence asset prices, with different implications for households according to what they own. Felix Nikolas Prehn, an economist and former investment banker, examines these distributional effects in *The Hidden Regressive Tax*, published by The Prehn Institute in September 2026. Available as a preprint on Zenodo, the report covers US monetary and household asset data from 2000 to 2026. Net interest in the fiscal 2026 budget The Treasury records net interest of $1,051,754 million for fiscal 2026, compared with $970,359 million a year earlier. That is an increase of about $81.4 billion, or 8.4 per cent. Total federal outlays reached $7,395,800 million, with the annual deficit at $1.992 trillion. Net interest measures federal interest costs after accounting offsets. The same statement reports gross interest on Treasury debt securities of $1,359,953 million. Gross interest records interest on Treasury securities before the adjustments reflected in net interest. Social Security totalled $1,667,097 million and Medicare $1,072,626 million, while the Health function was $1,025,587 million. Net interest therefore sat below Medicare but above Health; National Defense, at $965,160 million, was also below it. This is a fiscal measure of government expenditure, not a measure of household asset gains. The Prehn Institute’s research examines those gains through data on asset ownership and prices. The Prehn Institute on monetary expansion and asset prices Felix Nikolas Prehn examines two processes through which money balances expanded after 2008. Federal Reserve purchases of Treasury and mortgage-backed securities create reserves in the banking system. Deposits held by households and businesses can also increase through lending or government spending. From 2008 to 2014, much of the additional reserves remained at the Federal Reserve, while M2, a broad measure of money, grew by 49 per cent over six years. During 2020 and 2021, Treasury borrowing and spending coincided with extensive Federal Reserve bond purchases, and M2 rose 41 per cent over 25 months. The Prehn Institute’s analysis of asset prices sets out four channels: investors seeking higher yields after selling safer bonds, changes in expected interest rates, greater borrowing capacity for asset owners, and signals of continued central bank support. The report describes a lag between asset-price movements and consumer-price effects. That timing is central to its distributional analysis because a household holding shares or property has a different exposure to rising asset values from one relying mainly on wages, cash savings and rented housing. Asset ownership and the distribution of gains The Prehn Institute examines changes in household wealth using the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts. For the first quarter of 2020 to the second quarter of 2026, its incidence table assigns 36.7 per cent of the increase to the top 1 per cent of households and 2.8 per cent to the bottom 50 per cent. These figures describe the distribution of the recorded increase over that period. The report identifies three effects on households with relatively few assets. Cash and wages can lose purchasing power as consumer prices rise. Higher house and share prices increase the cost of becoming an owner, while existing owners may benefit from rising valuations. Households without those holdings receive little or none of the corresponding increase in asset values. Felix Nikolas Prehn examines these effects through the analogy of a monetary levy. A conventional tax has a stated rate and a record of collection; the report describes a process in which the economic burden emerges through price changes. As the paper puts it, “There is no rate; the size of the transfer emerges after the fact from the movement of prices.” The report’s incidence table is stylised, with approximate estimates for some middle wealth groups. It also acknowledges other influences on prices and household finances, including supply disruptions and fiscal transfers during the pandemic. The percentages should be read within those methodological limits. Interpreting the fiscal and household figures The Prehn Institute’s household analysis addresses a different question from the Treasury’s net-interest line. The fiscal statement reports spending by budget function, whereas the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts provide quarterly estimates of assets and liabilities across household groups. Establishing the recipients of a particular year’s federal interest payments would require evidence about the holders of Treasury securities. Fiscal 2026 covers the 12 months to September 2026, while the report’s selected household comparison extends from early 2020 to the second quarter of 2026. Shares of asset gains across that longer interval cannot be treated as a breakdown of the Treasury’s annual interest cost. The Prehn Institute’s proposed distinction separates changes in consumer prices from changes in asset prices when discussing inflation. Public attention during 2021 to 2023 focused on groceries, petrol and other household expenses, while the report examines earlier gains in the prices of shares and housing. Distinguishing the measures can clarify effects on current spending and the cost of acquiring assets. About Felix Nikolas Prehn Felix Nikolas Prehn, also known as Nikolas Prehn, is an economist and former investment banker, born in Germany. He is a tech founder: he co-founded TradeVision.io (Acetrader Inc), founded Winston Daily and The Prehn Institute, and publishes weekly on YouTube. He is also a painter and sculptor and a public advocate for animal rescue. About The Prehn Institute The Prehn Institute is an independent research institution founded by Felix Nikolas Prehn.
